caseStudies.title: Amazon Fashion Redesign
caseStudies.subtitle: Landing Page UX Redesign
caseStudies.tagline: Make choosing easier, not to show more things.
caseStudies.summary: Reimagine the Amazon Fashion landing page to make browsing easier and reduce decision fatigue.
caseStudies.brief: Reimagine the Amazon Fashion landing page to make browsing easier, reduce decision fatigue and help users discover products faster without limiting choice.
caseStudies.thinking: The redesign focuses on simplifying product discovery through clearer hierarchy, intuitive navigation and progressive exploration. By reducing visual clutter and organising content around customer intent...
caseStudies.myRole: Conducted research, identified user pain points, developed the UX strategy, designed user flows and wireframes, created the final UI and presented the design rationale.

caseStudies.title: Swiggy Instamart UX Overhaul
caseStudies.subtitle: 10-Minute Grocery — Zero-Friction Checkout
caseStudies.tagline: Speed is the feature. Every tap that slows you down is a broken promise.
caseStudies.summary: A ground-up UX audit and redesign of the Swiggy Instamart checkout flow — reducing friction from cart to confirmation by eliminating redundant steps and surfacing trust signals at the right moments.
caseStudies.context: Swiggy Instamart entered the 10-minute grocery delivery space with an aggressive promise — but the checkout experience hadn't kept up. Users were abandoning carts at the payment step, not because they didn't want to buy, but because the flow made them work too hard. The tension between speed-as-brand and slowness-as-UX was undercutting trust at the exact moment the product needed to deliver on its core promise.
caseStudies.problemStatement: How do we make the checkout feel as fast as the delivery — from cart to confirmation in under 4 taps?
goals: Surface coupons before the payment screen
Show persistent delivery ETA at every checkout step
Validate redesign via unmoderated usability testing (Maze)

researchMethods.name: Heuristic Audit
researchMethods.description: Mapped every screen of the existing checkout flow against Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics. Identified 3 major anti-patterns including forced address re-entry and buried coupon discovery.

researchMethods.name: Moderated Usability Sessions
researchMethods.description: 6 sessions (3 frequent users, 3 occasional buyers). Coded recordings for task failure and hesitation moments to identify the highest-friction points.

researchMethods.name: Affinity Mapping
researchMethods.description: Session findings synthesised in Miro into an affinity map revealing 3 core user frustrations: uncertainty, extra steps, and hidden value.

researchMethods.name: Competitor Analysis
researchMethods.description: Audited checkout flows of Blinkit, Zepto, and BigBasket to identify best-in-class patterns and industry benchmarks for quick-commerce checkout.

personas.name: Shreya, 27
personas.quote: I just want it to be done. I know what I want — don't make me re-confirm my address every single time.
painPoints: Coupons hidden until the payment screen
Too many steps between cart and confirmation

personas.name: Arjun, 34
personas.quote: I'm never sure my order actually went through until I see the confirmation. The whole thing feels uncertain.
painPoints: No reassurance during the checkout process
Payment page too cluttered — hard to verify order

ideation.approach: After research synthesis, three design principles emerged: progressive disclosure (show only what's needed at each step), persistent context (delivery ETA visible at all times), and a collapsed payment summary that consolidates address, slot, and payment into one scannable view. I sketched 6 layout directions and narrowed to 2 viable options before committing to the final direction.

solutions.title: Option A — Single-scroll checkout
solutions.description: Everything on one vertical scroll — cart, address, coupon, payment. Minimal taps but high cognitive load upfront. Testing showed users felt overwhelmed and skipped the coupon section entirely.

solutions.title: Option B — Progressive disclosure
solutions.description: Three focused screens: Cart → Address + Slot → Payment Summary. Each screen handles one decision. Chosen for its lower cognitive load, better error recovery, and significantly higher coupon discovery rate in early testing.

modules.name: Cart Screen
modules.description: Reorganised cart with a persistent ETA bar at the top, inline item editing, and coupon discovery moved above the fold — before the user even thinks about payment.

modules.name: Address & Delivery Slot
modules.description: Combined address confirmation and delivery slot selection into one screen. When the default slot is valid, it's pre-selected — the user can confirm in a single tap.

modules.name: Payment Summary
modules.description: A single-screen payment view consolidating address, delivery slot, order total, and payment method. The full order is visible and verifiable before the card is charged.

designSystem.credit: Built on top of Swiggy's existing design language and component library. Color tokens and typeface follow Swiggy's public brand guidelines.

userTesting.method: Unmoderated usability testing via Maze · n = 18 participants
changes: Added persistent delivery ETA bar — first-round participants expressed uncertainty about their delivery window mid-checkout
Moved coupon field above payment method — 4 of 6 first-round participants completely missed it at the bottom
Added item count badge to the confirmation header — 2 participants wanted to verify their cart before the order was finalised

conclusion.challenges: Working without access to Swiggy's real analytics meant every assumption had to be validated independently. The n=18 sample size is too small for statistical significance — findings are directional, not definitive. A real production test would require much larger sample sizes and instrumented analytics.
conclusion.outcomes: The redesigned prototype met all 4 project goals. Task completion improved from 71% to 94%, time-to-payment dropped by 38 seconds, and trust ratings for the confirmation screen jumped from 3.1 to 4.6 out of 5.
conclusion.learnings: The coupon placement discovery was the biggest surprise — it wasn't just a convenience issue, it was a trust issue. Users felt Swiggy was 'hiding' savings from them. In future projects I'd frame coupon and discount discoverability as a trust signal from the start, not purely a UX convenience.

futureScope: Integrate loyalty rewards directly within the cart screen (not as a separate post-purchase flow)
Personalised delivery slot suggestions based on a user's past order timing patterns
Voice-assisted checkout as an accessibility and speed improvement
A/B test the progressive disclosure flow vs. single-scroll approach with real production traffic
Saved address shortcuts for frequently used delivery locations (home, office)
